hero.headline: Vision Marine Technologies announces pending sale of Palm City property
hero.teaser: Vision Marine Technologies completed consolidation of its tender-rigging operations at a Fort Lauderdale marina and announced it plans to sell its Palm City property.
hero.body:
Vision Marine Technologies announced Tuesday it has completed consolidation of tender-rigging operations at its Fort Lauderdale marina location. The company also announced a pending sale of its Palm City property.

The marine technology company moved its tender operations from Palm City to Fort Lauderdale as part of the consolidation. The Palm City facility is now under contract for sale.

Vision Marine Technologies specializes in electric marine propulsion systems and boat manufacturing. The operational consolidation represents a restructuring of the company's South Florida facilities.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce commissioners reject lawsuit settlement over Little Jim Bait & Tackle waterfront dispute
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously Monday night to reject a settlement offer in a lawsuit alleging years of waterfront mismanagement tied to histo.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously Monday night to reject a settlement offer in a lawsuit alleging years of waterfront mismanagement tied to historic restaurant Little Jim Bait & Tackle. Plaintiff Kevin Keene said he will continue to pursue litigation against the city following the vote. The city has filed a motion to dismiss Keene's amended complaint. Under the proposed settlement terms, Keene would have dropped the case if the city halted any new plans for Little Jim until Florida Department of Environmental Protection permit issues are resolved and allowed a public vote on future waterfront land decisions. Documents obtained from the FDEP claim the city has been operating docks on state-owned submerged land at Little Jim without the required permits since 2021. The state agency has ordered the city to pay nearly $16,000 by July 17.

The dispute traces back to last year when the Fort Pierce landmark of nearly 80 years faced an uncertain future after its lease expired. The city offered up the land lease for bidders, much to the outcry of residents. After an outpouring of community support, the city kept the restaurant open month to month. The city said none of five formal proposals submitted, including one from the current operators, met the criteria and scrapped plans to pick a new tenant. Keene argues the Little Jim process was marked by instability, changing information and unresolved material issues, pointing to two other controversial city projects: Fisherman's Wharf, where state records show the city promised land it didn't own, and King's Landing, where a developer claims the city promised buildable property that contained 1,500 tons of old power plant concrete. City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the city is planning to hire a real estate manager to oversee development decisions.

cards.headline: Martin County School District plans to cut 16 administrative positions, save nearly $4 million
cards.teaser: The Martin County School District plans to cut district staff as part of a reorganization for the upcoming school year, saving nearly $4 million from next year's budget.
cards.body:
The Martin County School District plans to cut 16 administrative positions and eliminate dozens of unfilled teaching vacancies as part of a reorganization aimed at saving nearly $4 million in next year's budget.

Superintendent Michael Maine told WPTV the plan includes eliminating 16 administrative and district-level positions, which includes three assistant principal positions, and removing 42 unfilled instructional vacancies. Maine said 10 of those vacancies were held in reserve, contingent on increasing enrollment. The reorganization is eliminating positions that we felt, or I felt, are no longer needed at the district office, so that we brunt a majority of the reduction, Maine said. He explained that the cuts reflect how the district routinely manages staffing each year, saying this is a normal way the district operates by looking at projected student numbers and allocating positions accordingly. The changes are expected to save about $3.9 million from the district's projected budget next school year. For us, that's a lot of money for a district our size, Maine said.

The Martin County School District currently enrolls 16,000 students. Maine said the goal is to protect classroom resources while streamlining operations at the district level. We absolutely can streamline and become more efficient at the district office with taxpayer dollars to be able to do more with less at the district versus at individual school sites, Maine said. Maine described his approach to the reorganization simply, saying lean and mean is what I like to say.

Not everyone is fully on board with the scope of the cuts. Abigal, whose son will be a fourth grader at Jensen Beach Elementary this fall, said she values the small class sizes and close teacher relationships the district currently offers. The teachers have one-to-one interactions with the kids, they do a lot of different kinds of learning as well, Abigal said. She said she hopes the district is careful about how deep the cuts go. The children need, you know, the admin, they need the teachers, they need all the resources, as much as they can get, Abigal said.

cards.headline: Vero Beach homeowner says $9,000 insurance costs may force her to sell home
cards.teaser: Kelly Hagen says skyrocketing insurance costs may soon force her out of her Vero Beach home as premiums have jumped from $6,000 to $9,000 a year.
cards.body:
Kelly Hagen says her homeowners insurance for her Vero Beach home has jumped to $9,000 a year, which equals $750 a month on top of her mortgage payment. Her home has three bedrooms and two baths, is about 1,500 square feet and was built in 1994. The premiums climbed from $6,000 to $8,000 the next year and then to $9,000. Hagen says the financial pressure goes beyond the premium itself. Her insurance company requires impact windows, an expensive upgrade she has struggled to afford while working two jobs. She works a full-time job and then works Instacart nights and weekends. Her situation was made worse when she was turned away for a $10,000 My Safe Florida Home grant after it took too long to find a contractor.

Hagen said she can probably hang on just a couple more months with these increases in insurance, then she can't do it. She said she will have to leave her house and try to sell it, and leaving would be devastating. Stand Insurance, a new company in the market, is offering to help homeowners connect with affordable contractors and uses AI technology to study homes and pair homeowners with vendors to make repairs. Dan Preston, the CEO of Stand Insurance, said helping someone be safer is beneficial to everyone involved. Experts advise homeowners in similar situations to explore workable changes to their policy and shop around for lower premiums with other insurance companies.

cards.headline: DeSantis closes final bill-signing season after reshaping Florida law over eight years
cards.body:
Ron DeSantis has likely wrapped his final regular bill-signing season, closing one of his last major opportunities to shape Florida law from the governor's desk. With the new fiscal year underway and DeSantis term-limited from seeking another consecutive term, the regular lawmaking window for his administration is essentially closed, barring a future special session, emergency response or other extraordinary action. Florida's Constitution bars a governor who has served more than six years across two consecutive terms from being elected to the succeeding term.

A review of regular-session action shows the scale of DeSantis' eight years in office: 2,037 regular-session bills signed since 2019, along with 66 regular-session vetoes. His busiest year came in 2023, when 341 regular-session bills became law. His lightest was his first year, 2019, with 189. Those laws reshaped major parts of Florida life. Under DeSantis, Florida expanded school choice, with the governor signing HB 1 in 2023 to eliminate income restrictions and open scholarship programs more broadly to students across the state. He also signed new abortion restrictions, including Florida's six-week ban, after first approving a 15-week restriction earlier in his tenure. The list includes permitless carry, expanded immigration enforcement, COVID-era limits on vaccine and mask mandates, new election laws, restrictions on diversity, equity and inclusion programs, and major property insurance changes. DeSantis also signed 2026 legislation giving Florida new authority tied to terrorist organization designations and additional limits on local DEI programs, continuing a broader conservative policy push in his final years in office. That agenda became central to the national brand DeSantis promoted as the Florida blueprint, a fast-moving conservative policy model powered by Republican control of the Legislature and the governor's office.

DeSantis used his veto power to block dozens of bills. In 2022, he vetoed a net-metering bill that critics said would have hurt rooftop solar customer incentives. That same year, DeSantis vetoed an alimony overhaul, citing concerns about retroactivity. In 2024, he vetoed hemp restrictions, arguing the bill would impose heavy regulatory burdens on small businesses. In 2026, he vetoed a sovereign immunity bill that would have increased lawsuit limits against state and local government entities.

Over eight years, DeSantis vetoed roughly $10.6 billion in spending, using Florida's line-item veto power to cut local projects, trim legislative priorities and reinforce his image as a fiscal conservative. In June, DeSantis signed a $117.6 billion budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year after nearly $810 million in line-item vetoes, with his office calling it the fourth straight year of declining state spending. Democrats and local officials have often criticized those cuts, arguing they hit community projects, infrastructure needs and social services. After more than 2,000 regular-session bills signed, 66 regular-session vetoes and billions cut from state spending, DeSantis leaves behind a Florida lawbook that looks far different than the one he inherited in 2019.

cards.headline: St. Lucie man with pancreatic cancer approved for experimental treatment after 62-day wait
cards.teaser: A St. Lucie man battling pancreatic cancer is sharing his story after finally gaining access to an experimental treatment his family hopes will give him more time.
cards.body:
For 64-year-old Russell Reed, the past two months have been filled with uncertainty. Reed spent 62 days waiting to learn whether he would be approved to receive daraxonrasib, an experimental drug his oncologist believed could help after traditional treatments were no longer effective. Daraxonrasib, also known as RMC-6236, is an investigational once-daily oral pill developed by Revolution Medicines. The drug targets mutated KRAS proteins, which drive more than 90% of pancreatic cancers. Reed said research and clinical trial results gave him hope that daraxonrasib could help slow the progression of his disease.

According to Reed's family, his oncologist submitted a request through the FDA's Expanded Access Program, which can allow patients with serious or life-threatening illnesses to receive treatments outside of clinical trials when other options are limited. Just two days after sharing their story with WPTV, Reed learned he had been approved to receive the treatment. The drug is now in his hands, and his family says he is already feeling better and optimistic about what comes next. Reed said there is a lot of anecdotal evidence and evidence from clinical trials that show this is the miracle drug for pancreatic cancer. It is not a cure, but it will give him time, he said.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound getting first Aldi grocery store July 9 at former Winn-Dixie site
hero.teaser: Hobe Sound will get its first Aldi store when the grocery chain opens July 9 at 8867 SE Bridge Road in the space where Winn-Dixie used to be.
hero.body:
Hobe Sound will get its first Aldi store when the grocery chain opens July 9 at 8867 SE Bridge Road in the space where Winn-Dixie used to be. Aldi has converted multiple Winn-Dixie stores across South Florida over the past few years. There will be a grand opening and ribbon-cutting ceremony on July 9 at 8:30 a.m.

The first 200 customers will receive a gift bag with Aldi products and a gift card. The Hobe Sound Aldi will be open daily from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.

hero.headline: IOC ends neutral status vetting for Russian athletes ahead of 2028 LA Olympics
hero.teaser: The International Olympic Committee advised Olympic sports bodies on Tuesday to end a three-year program vetting Russians for neutral status ahead of qualifying events for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
hero.body:
The IOC advised Olympic sports bodies on Tuesday to end a three-year program vetting Russians for neutral status ahead of qualifying events for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. The move was expected since the International Olympic Committee advised two months ago that athletes from Belarus, Russia's military ally in the full military invasion of Ukraine, should be allowed again to compete with their full national identity. "The IOC stands in solidarity with the Olympic community of Ukraine, which the Olympic movement has supported since the beginning of the war, and will continue to do so," the Olympic body said in a statement after a meeting of its executive board.

The IOC eased entry requirements to its own events for Russian athletes and teams while provisionally lifting its suspension since October 2023 of the Russian Olympic Committee. The terms of that suspension, which was imposed when the Russian Olympic body incorporated regional sports councils from occupied regions of Ukraine, no longer applied, the IOC said. Just 32 athletes from Russia and Belarus competed at the 2024 Paris Olympics as approved neutrals and combined to win five medals. The Russian team had more than 300 athletes at the 2021 Tokyo Olympics and won 71 medals.

The IOC did not yet approve letting Russian athletes and teams compete with their flag and anthem. That decision will come at an appropriate time, the organization said. The next Olympic competition is the 2026 Youth Summer Games in Dakar, Senegal opening Oct. 31. The IOC said to address the lack of confidence in the global sporting community relating to the return of Russian athletes to international competition, those athletes must give multiple doping controls and be part of a recognized testing program.

The IOC also said it will continue to not organize IOC events in Russia or invite Russian government or state officials to its events. The decision marks a significant shift in the Olympic body's approach to Russian participation following the invasion of Ukraine, though restrictions remain in place regarding national symbols and official representation. The provisional lifting of the Russian Olympic Committee's suspension represents a step toward normalizing Russian participation in Olympic sports, while the organization maintains its stated support for the Ukrainian Olympic community.

cards.headline: United States eliminated from World Cup in 4-1 loss to Belgium in Seattle
cards.teaser: The United States lost 4-1 to Belgium on Monday night at Lumen Field in Seattle, ending American hopes for a World Cup title on home soil.
cards.body:
The United States' hopes for a deep World Cup run at home ended when Charles De Ketelaere scored twice and assisted on another goal, helping Belgium expose the Americans' defensive liabilities in a 4-1 win Monday night that earned a quarterfinal berth. American defenders were at fault in a pair of first-half goals and goalkeeper Matt Freese's gaffe gave the Red Devils a third early in the second half. Second-half substitute Romelu Lukaku added Belgium's final goal in the third minute of stoppage time. Belgium knocked the U.S. out in the round of 16 for the second time in 12 years and extended its unbeaten streak to 18 games. The Red Devils play 2010 champion Spain on Friday at Inglewood, California, for a semifinal berth.

Malik Tillman tied the score 1-1 midway through the first half with his second free kick goal of the tournament, but the Americans conceded just 61 seconds after the ensuing kickoff. Coach Mauricio Pochettino showed his frustration by kicking a rack in front of the bench, sending four water bottles flying. American star Christian Pulisic injured his right foot when he hit a boot of Belgium captain Youri Tielemans on a 52nd-minute shot attempt and was replaced seven minutes later. A crowd of 66,925 at Lumen Field watched De Ketelaere put Belgium ahead in the eighth minute. After winning three games in the expanded 48-nation tournament, the U.S. failed to reach the quarterfinals for the first time since 2002.

cards.headline: Serena Williams withdraws from Wimbledon doubles with sister Venus due to knee injury
cards.teaser: Serena Williams withdrew from her doubles match with sister Venus at Wimbledon on Saturday due to a right knee injury suffered during her singles return earlier in the week.
cards.body:
Serena Williams withdrew from her doubles match with sister Venus at Wimbledon on Saturday due to a right knee injury. The 44-year-old Serena was injured during her singles return earlier in the week in a three-set loss. She posted on Instagram that she was heartbroken to have to withdraw from doubles and that coming back to compete again has been a gift. The post included images of four syringes that Serena said shows the fluid they drained from her knee after her singles match. An accompanying video showed her walking with strapping up and down her right leg and what appeared to be one of her daughters holding a cane for her.

The Williams sisters were scheduled to play Camila Osorio and Solana Sierra. It was the only first-round doubles match that wasn't scheduled earlier in the week, having been pushed back to give Serena more time to recover. Serena was beaten 6-3, 6-7 (6), 6-3 by 20-year-old Maya Joint of Australia on Tuesday. Venus, who is 46, played in the mixed doubles tournament on Friday together with Kevin Krawietz, losing in straight sets to Tereza Mihalikova and Lloyd Glasspool. The Williams sisters are six-time champions as partners in women's doubles at Wimbledon. With the U.S. Open approaching, Serena indicated she could play again somewhere else soon, saying to stay tuned to a city near you.

hero.headline: 18th Annual Treasure Coast Seafood Festival Returns to Vero Beach This November
hero.body:
Under The Sun Promotions, Inc. has announced the return of the 18th Annual Treasure Coast Seafood Festival to Vero Beach this November. The event marks nearly two decades of the regional seafood celebration in Indian River County.

The festival is scheduled to take place in Vero Beach during November 2026. Under The Sun Promotions, Inc. is organizing the annual event.

The Treasure Coast Seafood Festival has become a recurring attraction for the region, drawing visitors to Vero Beach each year. The November timing places the festival during the fall season when coastal Florida typically sees increased tourism activity.

This year's festival will mark the 18th consecutive year the event has been held. Additional details about specific dates, location, vendors, and activities will be released as the November event date approaches.

cards.headline: Florida minimum wage workers need nearly 26 years to save for home down payment
cards.teaser: A new study shows it now takes the median-income household in Florida 17 months longer to save for a down payment than it did a decade ago.
cards.body:
For Floridians dreaming of owning a home, saving for a down payment remains a heavy burden. A new study by Smart Asset quantifies just how heavy a burden it is. The study found that, on average, it now takes the median-income household earner in Florida 17 months longer to save up for a down payment in 2026 than in 2016, considerably longer than it did a decade ago. According to Smart Asset, for Floridians who earn a minimum wage of $14 an hour, it takes nearly 26 years to save up for a down payment on a home.

Florida was No. 25 on this list, while residents in Idaho have been affected the most in the last 10 years. Residents of Idaho now need 40 months longer to buy a home than in 2016. Only in three states, Louisiana, Mississippi and North Dakota, can median-income households save a down payment faster than they could in 2016. The report found that West Virginia has the nation's lowest down payment burden. A median-income household in West Virginia needs 5.5 years to save for a down payment in 2026, just three months longer than in 2016. According to the study, saving for a down payment on a minimum-wage income alone is essentially impossible in every state.

hero.headline: Vision Marine Technologies announces pending sale of Palm City property
hero.teaser: Vision Marine Technologies completed consolidation of its tender-rigging operations at a Fort Lauderdale marina and announced it plans to sell its Palm City property.
hero.body:
Vision Marine Technologies announced Tuesday it has completed consolidation of tender-rigging operations at its Fort Lauderdale marina location. The company also announced a pending sale of its Palm City property.

The marine technology company moved its tender operations from Palm City to Fort Lauderdale as part of the consolidation. The Palm City facility is now under contract for sale.

Vision Marine Technologies specializes in electric marine propulsion systems and boat manufacturing. The operational consolidation represents a restructuring of the company's South Florida facilities.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County pancreatic cancer patient approved for experimental drug after 62-day wait
hero.body:
Russell Reed, a 64-year-old St. Lucie County man battling pancreatic cancer, has gained access to an experimental treatment after waiting 62 days for approval. Reed received authorization to use daraxonrasib, an investigational once-daily oral pill, after his oncologist determined that traditional treatments were no longer effective. The drug, also known as RMC-6236, is manufactured by Revolution Medicines and targets mutated KRAS proteins that drive more than 90% of pancreatic cancers.

Reed's oncologist submitted a request through the FDA's Expanded Access Program, which can allow patients with serious or life-threatening illnesses to receive treatments outside of clinical trials when other options are limited. While daraxonrasib is not yet FDA-approved, early clinical trial results have generated optimism among some patients and physicians. Reed said research and clinical trial results gave him hope the drug could help slow the progression of his disease. "There's a lot of anecdotal evidence and a lot of evidence from the clinical trials that show that this is the miracle drug for pancreatic cancer," Reed said. "It is not a cure, but it will give me time."

During the two-month wait for approval, Reed and his wife Marnie focused on making the most of their time together rather than dwelling on uncertainty. "The idea of sitting here and waiting for the phone to ring is not ok with me," Marnie Reed said, explaining that her husband needed attention and engagement. For Marnie, the fight extended beyond simply accessing a drug. It was about creating more family trips, memories and moments together. "You're still here, and if you don't pay attention, you're going to miss it," she said. "I don't want to miss a minute with him."

Just two days after sharing their story with WPTV, Reed received the call informing him of his approval to receive the treatment. The drug is now in his hands, and his family says he is already feeling better and optimistic about what comes next. While daraxonrasib is not considered a cure for pancreatic cancer, the Reeds say the approval represents what they have been fighting for all along: more time together. Reed acknowledged the limitations of the experimental treatment but remained hopeful about its potential to extend his life with his family.

cards.headline: Construction underway on 18-hole golf course at Esplanade at Solaeris in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: Taylor Morrison has begun construction on a Wilczynski-designed 18-hole golf course at its new Esplanade at Solaeris residential community in Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
Construction has started on an 18-hole golf course at Esplanade at Solaeris, Taylor Morrison's new golf residential community in Port St. Lucie. The course was designed by Wilczynski.

The development represents Taylor Morrison's expansion into the Port St. Lucie golf community market. The golf course will serve as the centerpiece amenity for the Esplanade at Solaeris residential community.

cards.headline: Legacy High School Named New Voting Location for Precinct 90 Voters in Tradition
cards.teaser: Legacy High School will serve as a new voting location for voters in Precinct 90 during the Primary Election on August 18, 2026, according to St. Lucie County Supervisor of Electio
cards.body:
Legacy High School will serve as a new voting location for voters in Precinct 90 during the Primary Election on August 18, 2026, according to St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker.

The school, located at 14505 Crosstown Parkway in Port St. Lucie, will serve voters who live north of Crosstown Parkway in the Tradition area.

Precinct 90 voters previously cast ballots at Tradition Town Hall, which is Precinct 89. Since the 2024 General Election, the voter population in the area has grown, prompting the Supervisor of Elections Office to search for an additional voting site.

Walker said the office worked with the St. Lucie County School District to secure Legacy High School as the new precinct location.

"We are grateful to the School District and Legacy High School for their commitment to serving this community," the Supervisor of Elections Office said.

The office said it is still searching for an Early Voting site to serve Tradition's rapidly growing population. Officials said the addition of Legacy High School as a precinct location is intended to help reduce Election Day wait times and ease pressure on Early Voting at the Paula A. Lewis Library.

Voters in Precinct 90 will receive mailed notifications from the Supervisor of Elections Office about the change to their assigned voting location.

For additional information, voters can contact the St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 or visit www.stlucievotes.gov.

hero.headline: Vero Beach homeowner may sell after insurance costs hit $9,000 a year
hero.body:
A Vero Beach homeowner says skyrocketing insurance costs may soon force her out of her home. Kelly Hagen says her homeowners insurance is $9,000 a year, which equates to $750 a month on top of her mortgage payment. Her home has three bedrooms and two baths, is about 1,500 square feet and was built in 1994. The insurance went from $6,000 to $8,000 the following year, and Hagen says it just keeps going up and up.

Hagen says the financial pressure goes beyond the premium itself. Her insurance company requires impact windows, an expensive upgrade she has struggled to afford while working two jobs. Hagen works a full-time job and then works Instacart nights and weekends. Her situation was made worse when she was turned away for a $10,000 My Safe Florida Home grant after it took too long to find a contractor, a roadblock many Florida homeowners have faced.

State leaders say now is the time for homeowners to shop around, pointing to new insurers entering the market with competitive rates. One new company, Stand Insurance, is offering to help homeowners connect with affordable contractors. Stand uses AI technology to study homes and then works to pair homeowners with vendors and contractors to make repairs. Dan Preston, the CEO of Stand Insurance, said if you can actually help someone be safer and have their home be safer, it's beneficial to everyone involved because the company does not have to pay out in claims and customers pay less in premiums.

When asked how much longer she can hang on with these increases in insurance, Hagen said probably just a couple more months, and then she cannot do it. She said she is going to have to leave her house and will have to try and sell her house. Leaving would be devastating, Hagen said. Experts advise homeowners in similar situations to explore workable changes to their policy and shop around for lower premiums with other insurance companies.
